tier_reason: Third-party bench-v8 v7 table by the QuickJS author (Chinese mirror of bellard.org/quickjs/bench.html) has XS 8.8.0 and Duktape 2.3.0 columns with every number in the record; benchmark code is the bench-v8 suite run by the bellard/quickjs Makefile target bench-v8 (tests/bench-v8, shipped in the quickjs-extras archive), gcc 4.9.2, -O3 for XS and -O2 for Duktape, Core i5 4570 stated. Same page and tier as the already-verified QuickJS entry.

corrections.license: XS engine sources (xs/sources) are LGPL-3.0-or-later and incorporate Apache-2.0 code from Kinoma/Marvell; SDK build tools GPL-3.0, examples CC-BY-4.0, some fonts OFL-1.1 (licenses/readme.md); a commercial licence is also offered
corrections.caveats: Benchmark was run by the QuickJS author in 2019 on XS 8.8.0, a much older version than today's; XS lost two of seven tests (Splay, NavierStokes) to Duktape and could not run RegExp. On the same table XS is clearly slower than QuickJS (738 vs 1138 total without RegExp, derived from page data about 0.65x), and QuickJS is also a baseline of this category, so the win holds only against Duktape. XS was built at -O3 while Duktape was built at -O2. The XS engine lives under xs/ inside the Moddable SDK repository. First-party performance claims by Moddable were not found.

notes: Numbers verified exactly on the mirror page (738/468 = about 1.6x, derived from page data); original bellard.org page is EGRESS_BLOCKED here. Shortcomings to record: 2019 numbers on XS 8.8.0, slower than QuickJS on the same table, flag mismatch (-O3 vs -O2), RegExp not runnable.

tier_reason: github.com/fwsGonzo/libriscv now serves the canonical libriscv/libriscv repository (1.1k stars, BSD-3-Clause), already verified at tier C; the two first-party gists carry the quoted numbers but state no compiler, flags, Luau/LuaJIT version or libriscv mode (the LuaJIT gist names an AMD Ryzen 7 6860Z).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Luau gist (https://gist.github.com/fwsGonzo/5ac8f4d8ca84e97b0c527aec76a86fe9): call overhead 2 ns vs 87 ns, integer math 3 ns vs 38 ns, fib(40) 220 ns vs 489 ns, syscall memcpy 18 ns vs 2170 ns, sieve(10M) 138 ms vs 574 ms. LuaJIT gist (https://gist.github.com/fwsGonzo/1af5b2a9b4f38c1f3d3074d78acdf609, AMD Ryzen 7 6860Z): call overhead 3 ns vs 196 ns, integer math 3 ns vs 85 ns, sieve(10M) 225 ms vs 241 ms, syscall memcpy 22 ns vs LuaJIT memcpy 117 ns; LuaJIT wins fib(40) (101 ns vs 167 ns), taylor(1K) (1038 ns vs 7875 ns) and plain memcpy against libriscv's naive guest memcpy (117 ns vs 1222 ns).

notes: Duplicate of https://github.com/libriscv/libriscv (same repository under its old owner path; duplicate decision already recorded). Gist numbers check out; the record omitted the taylor(1K) row where LuaJIT is about 7.6x faster (derived from page data).

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: an independent measurement by Elmar Klausmeier (blog post of 14 May 2020, read via its GitHub Pages source eklausme/eklausme.github.io) times Pallene against Lua 5.4, Lua 5.1-5.3, LuaJIT and C on an AMD FX-8120 with gcc 9.3.0, with the n-queens code public in eklausme/c (xdamcnt2.pln/.lua/.c) and the array program inline; not A because Pallene and Lua build flags are not stated. The peer-reviewed SBLP 2018 / SCP 2020 papers also report the win but could only be seen as search snippets.

corrections.baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.4 interpreter (the Lua 5.4 bundled with Pallene in 2020); LuaJIT and C in the same post
corrections.workload: Independent blog: n-queens counter xdamcnt2 (N up to 12, non-recursive, code in github.com/eklausme/c) and an array-of-records float update loop (N=4000, S=1000), each in Pallene, Lua and C. Paper (snippet only): binarytrees, binsearch, centroid, conway, matmul, queen, sieve and others from the repo benchmarks directory.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Klausmeier blog (2020): n-queens Pallene 0.32 s (0.31 s with compiler optimization flags) vs Lua 5.4 3.92 s (about 12x, derived from page data; the post says 13x) and vs LuaJIT 0.58 s (about 1.8x, derived from page data), C -O3 0.2 s; array loop Pallene 0.14 s vs Lua 5.4 0.72 s (about 5x, derived from page data), but LuaJIT 0.07 s is 2x faster than Pallene there. Paper (SBLP 2018 / SCP 2020, search snippets only): around ten times faster than Lua on Sieve and Queens, comparable to LuaJIT; more than three times faster than LuaJIT and the Lua-C API on binary search; LuaJIT substantially faster only on Matmul (NaN-boxing gives 8-byte floats vs 16 bytes in Lua and Pallene).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 on Arch Linux 5.6.6; the C reference built with -march=native -O3; Pallene and Lua 5.4 build flags not stated (a second Pallene run 'with compiler optimization flags' does not name them)
corrections.hardware: AMD FX-8120 eight-core, 3.1 GHz max (blog); paper hardware unknown
corrections.caveats: Independent numbers are from one 2020 blog post on two small programs with a 2020 Pallene (older syntax) and an AMD FX-8120; Pallene and Lua flags unstated. LuaJIT beats Pallene 2x on the array-of-records loop and, per the paper snippets, on Matmul. The peer-reviewed papers (inf.puc-rio.br, ScienceDirect, ReadKong mirror) and the 2020 PhD thesis are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so paper numbers are snippet only. The README gives no figures and the repo benchmarks directory has code (benchmarks/run, benchlib.lua) but no results. Pallene is a Lua companion language compiled to C Lua modules, not a C/C++ library.

notes: Upgrade to B on the Klausmeier independent measurement (blog mirror at raw.githubusercontent.com/eklausme/eklausme.github.io, code in eklausme/c). Shortcomings to record: LuaJIT faster on array loop and Matmul, flags unstated, 2020 version, paper numbers snippet only. Metadata (839 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-09-30) confirmed.
